1: Good morning everyone. My name is Yasir Alyoubi. My principal supervisor is Professor Farookh Hussain, and my co-supervisor is Dr Firas Al-Doghman. This is my candidature reassessment. My research asks one simple question. When a doctor asks for a patient's data, how can the system be sure that this request is really allowed? Not just who is asking. Also, did the patient and the guardians agree? Is the request inside the agreed data? And is the consent still valid today? I will show you the problem, what the literature says, my framework, the working prototype, and the results.
2: Here is the plan for my talk. First, the problem. Then the literature review. Then the gaps, the questions and the objectives. After that, the framework and its six steps. Then the validation and the evaluation results. Then I talk about what is still open and the research plan. At the end, I show a demonstration of the prototype through the slides: one real consent, from the day it is created to the day it is revoked.
3: Let me start with the problem. Health data is very sensitive. One decision to share it can involve many people: the patient, one or more guardians, the doctor, and the hospital. Today, consent is usually just a record that is saved somewhere. That record says permission was given. But it does not check anything when someone asks for the data. A valid login does not mean you have the right to see this patient's data. And even with approval, a request can ask for more data than the patient allowed, or it can come after the consent has expired or was cancelled. So the real problem is this: there is no single trusted decision that checks all of these things together.
4: Here is my answer in simple words. Consent should not be a record that we store. It should be an object that the system checks every time. I call this object C, and it has six parts. I is identity: who is involved. A is authority: which guardians must approve, and how many. P is policy: the purpose and the data that was agreed. T is time: when the consent starts and when it ends. L is jurisdiction: where the request may come from. And E is evidence: the signatures, the token, and whether the consent was cancelled. At every request, the system checks all six parts. If one part fails, the answer is no.
5: This is how I did the literature review. I followed the PRISMA 2020 method. Before I started screening, I wrote a protocol that fixed the questions, the databases, one search query, the criteria and the quality items. I searched seven databases. They gave me 9,256 records. After I removed duplicates, 6,039 were screened by title, 3,129 by abstract, and 1,800 full texts were put in order of priority. At the reporting checkpoint, 64 full texts were assessed and 47 met the criteria. From these, I analysed 25 primary studies in depth: 23 core studies and 2 supporting studies.
6: This figure sums up the review. The good news: every requirement is covered by some study. The problem: no study puts all the conditions together in one access decision. I call this the conjunction gap. And no study proves or tests the whole decision. Formal proofs exist in only 4 of the 25 studies, and they cover only a small part. I call this the assurance gap. These two gaps are what my research fills.
7: From the 25 studies, I found six gaps. One gap for each requirement. Gap one: consent is only a record. Gap two: identity does not prove authority. Gap three: multi-party approval is not a condition of every access. Gap four: purpose and scope are rarely checked together with identity and approval. Gap five: time and revocation are often checked only once, at registration, not at each request. Gap six: nobody proves or tests the whole decision.
8: So this is my main research question. How can a trust-oriented computing framework establish and enforce trustworthy multi-party consent for decentralised healthcare data sharing, under identity, authority and policy constraints? It has six sub-questions, one for each gap. How to model consent. How to check identity and authority. How several guardians can approve together. How purpose and scope are checked. How time and lifecycle are checked. And how to prove and test the security.
9: Each question has one objective. RO1 to RO4 are done, and they are validated with the prototype. RO5 is time and lifecycle. It is in progress. The validity window and the revocation already work. Consent changes, delegation and guardian changes are for the next stage. RO6 is partly completed. The automated tests, the attack tests and the measurements are done. The formal proofs are for the next stage.
10: These are the steps I followed. Step one, I identified the problem. Step two, I did the systematic review. Step three, from the review I found the gaps and wrote the questions. Step four, I set the objectives. Step five, I designed the framework: the architecture, the consent object, and four algorithms. Step six, I built the prototype on the Sepolia test network. Step seven, I evaluated it with live scenarios, measurements and attack tests. The formal proofs are the next stage.
11: The framework uses the Model, View, Controller pattern. The View is the four screens: patient, guardian, doctor and auditor. The View never decides who gets access. Every security decision is made in the Controller. It checks identity and authority, collects the approvals, enforces the policy, and records the evidence. The Model keeps the consent, the approvals and the evidence. Health data is released only when the Controller says ALLOW.
12: This is the heart of the framework. Access is allowed only when five checks are all true. VI: the identity and the authority are valid. VA: all the required guardians approved, the token exists, and the consent is not cancelled. VP: the purpose and the requested data are inside what was agreed. VT: the request is inside the validity time. VL: the jurisdiction matches. If any one check fails, the answer is DENY. In the prototype, a Groth16 zero-knowledge proof must also pass before any data is released. And every decision on an active consent is written to the audit ledger.
13: Step one. The patient creates the consent. The patient chooses the doctor, the guardians, the data modules, the start and end time, and the jurisdiction. The system checks every field. For example, an empty data scope or a bad guardian DID is rejected. Then the consent object C is built and saved as pending. Nothing goes to the blockchain yet. This is RO1, and it is done.
14: Step two. I separate two questions: who are you, and what may you do? The DID answers the first question. The credential answers the second. A valid identity alone never gives access. To be clear about the current state: today the prototype checks the DID format and recovers each guardian's signature. Full DID resolution and credential validation are planned for the next stage. So RO2 is done at the design level and in the prototype.
15: Step three. No single person can approve alone. Each guardian signs with an EIP-712 signature. The system recovers the signer and checks that this person is one of the listed guardians. Outsiders, replays and duplicates are not counted. In the demo, two of two guardians must sign. When both have signed, a soulbound token is minted on the Sepolia test network in the background. One honest note: in the prototype, the guardian keys are derived from the guardian DIDs. Wallet-held keys are for the next stage. RO3 is done.
16: Step four. A valid identity and all the approvals are still not enough. The requested data must be inside the agreed data scope. For example, if the consent allows Observation and Medication, a request that also asks for Procedure is denied. The purpose, the time and the jurisdiction are checked in the same decision. And a Groth16 proof must pass before any data is released. RO4 is done.
17: Step five. Time and lifecycle. What works now: the validity window is stored on-chain and checked at every request. Revocation works end to end, with an on-chain transaction. And the consent moves through a clear lifecycle. What is still open: the lifecycle transition check, consent modification, delegation, changes to the guardian set, and a formal lifecycle model. That is why RO5 is in progress.
18: Step six. Prove it and test it. The testing part is done. 36 automated tests pass, including twelve attack scenarios. I also measured the cost and the timing. The proof part is the next stage: formal proofs or model checking of the security properties, and a bigger evaluation under load. That is why RO6 is partly completed.
19: Validation asks one question: does the system do what it should? I used five kinds of evidence. Valid scenarios: the correct requests were allowed. Negative scenarios: the wrong jurisdiction and the cancelled consent were refused. Attack scenarios: eleven of twelve attacks are refused after the hardening. Automated tests: all 36 pass. And an independent check: the state on the chain matches the local state.
20: I also attacked my own system twelve times. For example, a signer who is not a guardian. A replayed or duplicate approval. A request outside the data scope. An expired or cancelled consent. A tampered proof. Before the hardening on the first of October, three attacks got through when the service functions were called directly. After the hardening, eleven of twelve are refused. The last one, A11, changes a stored digest. The prototype does not compare that digest yet, so it is marked neutral. It is on the list for the next stage.
21: Evaluation asks: how fast is it, and what does it cost? The decision rule itself takes about 2 microseconds. One guardian signature takes about 11 milliseconds. The Groth16 proof is the slowest part: about 1.4 seconds to generate and about half a second to verify. Anchoring on Sepolia takes about 11.5 seconds, but it runs in the background, so nobody waits for it. A revoke uses about one sixth of the gas of a mint. The timings were measured on the first of October 2026. The gas and the anchoring times come from the five Sepolia transactions in September. These numbers are indicative.
22: Here is the difference in plain words. Today, a central identity provider logs you in, and a fixed permission decides. Consent is a saved record. In HALAH, every person has a DID, and identity is separate from authority. Consent is an object that is checked at every request. All the guardians must approve. Five checks and a proof run before any data is released. Time and revocation are checked every time. And every decision on an active consent is logged with the reason.
23: A few important points about the data. I use synthetic patient records from the Synthea 1K sample, in its CSV export. The prototype loads a subset of patients with their observations, conditions, medications and procedures. No real patient data is involved. The medical records stay off-chain. The token on Sepolia stores only pseudonymous addresses, a hash of the purpose, the validity window, a jurisdiction code and a revocation flag. Data is released only on ALLOW, and only inside the agreed scope. One known limitation: the plain-text purpose is visible in the mint transaction. I will fix this in the next stage.
24: Why does this matter? On the scientific side: consent becomes an object that is checked, not stored. Multi-party approval is a condition of every access. Identity is separated from authority. And the whole decision is checked in one place and tested. On the social side: patients and guardians decide together who sees the data. No single person can approve alone. Every decision can be explained to an auditor. And medical records never go on the blockchain.
25: I want to be clear about what is not done yet, because this is what the next stage is for. First, the formal proofs. The properties are tested, but not yet proved with a formal model. Second, the rest of the lifecycle: consent modification, delegation and guardian changes. Third, full DID resolution, credential validation and wallet-held guardian keys. Today it is a format check, a signature, and keys derived from the guardian DIDs. Fourth, the one open attack, A11. Fifth, a bigger evaluation under load. Sixth, the plain-text purpose in the mint transaction.
26: This is the plan. Chapters one to six are done. The conference paper was submitted to BWCCA 2026 in September. The SLR journal paper is in progress. Next comes the complete evaluation, the paper on formal assurance and lifecycle trust, and the conclusion. The final assessment is planned for January 2027, and the thesis submission for March 2027.
27: This is the same plan as a timeline. What is completed, what is in progress, and the planned steps up to the thesis submission in March 2027.
28: Now the demonstration, through the slides. HALAH means History Access Link for Authorised Healthcare. These are its parts: four screens, a soulbound token contract on the Sepolia test network, EIP-712 guardian signatures, a Groth16 proof at access time, synthetic data, and an audit ledger. In the next slides, I walk you through one real consent, from creation to revocation. What you will see covers RO1 to RO4 in full, and the parts of RO5 and RO6 that already work.
29: Demo step one. The patient creates the consent. On this screen you can see the four data modules, the two guardians, the jurisdiction AU, and the state PENDING_SIGNATURE. The system checked every field before saving. Nothing has gone to the blockchain yet. This is RO1: consent as an object the system can check.
30: Demo step two. The first guardian signs. The system takes the EIP-712 signature, finds who signed it, and confirms that this address is one of the two listed guardians. The counter shows one of two. The consent is still pending, because one approval is never enough. This is RO3.
31: Demo step three. The second guardian signs. Now the threshold, two of two, is reached. The system records the token locally and starts the mint on Sepolia in the background. The guardian does not wait for the blockchain. On the right, the same screen a bit later: already anchored on Sepolia, with the token number. RO3 is complete.
32: Demo step four. The doctor asks for the patient's data. First the proof is generated and verified. Then the five checks run. Identity and authority, VI. Approvals and token, VA. Purpose and scope, VP. Time, VT. Jurisdiction, VL. All five pass, so the answer is ALLOW. This is RO2 and RO4 together, in one decision.
33: Demo step five. After ALLOW, the records are shown per module. Only the modules inside the consent scope are returned. If the doctor asked for a module that was not agreed, the request would be refused. That case is covered by attack test A4. The decision and its matrix are written to the audit ledger.
34: Demo step six. The same doctor repeats the request, but this time declares the jurisdiction as SA. The consent was issued for AU. Everything else passes, but VL fails. One failed check is enough: access is denied. The message tells the auditor exactly which check failed. This is the rule of RO4 in action.
35: Demo step seven. The patient cancels the consent. On the left, the system is sending the revoke transaction to Sepolia and waiting for the block confirmation. On the right, the consent is now REVOKED, with its token number. This is the working part of RO5.
36: Demo step eight. The doctor tries again. Now VA fails, because the consent is not active any more: its state is REVOKED. Access is refused. An expired consent is refused in the same way, through the time check VT. So a consent that was valid yesterday does not stay usable forever.
37: Demo step nine. Both the mint and the revoke are public transactions on Sepolia. On the left, the anchoring transaction of the consent, in block 11,771,243. On the right, the revocation, in block 11,771,307, with the decoded function revoke and token id 1. Anyone can check them. No medical data is on the chain.
38: Demo step ten, the last one. The auditor can rebuild the full life of the consent: thirteen events in order, from creation to revocation, each with its decision matrix. The dashboard shows the exported ledger: 60 events, 9 access requests and 5 on-chain anchors. And a separate tool re-checked Sepolia and found every anchored transaction in its recorded block. All checks passed. This is the working part of RO6: evidence that can be audited.

45:
Thank you for listening. I am happy to take your questions.

Likely questions and short answers:
1. Why blockchain, if the data stays off-chain? Because it gives a shared record that cannot be changed quietly: the consent state and the revocation. No medical data is on the chain.
2. What is new? The consent object carries all the conditions. Multi-party approval is a condition of every access. And the whole decision is tested against attacks.
3. Why is RO6 only partly done? The testing is done. The formal proofs are the next stage.
4. Why Groth16? The doctor proves that they know the secret and the expiry behind the commitment stored in the consent, and that the consent has not expired, without showing them. It is the slowest part, about 1.4 seconds, and that is fine for a consent decision.
5. Why did three attacks pass before the hardening? They passed only when the service functions were called directly, not through the screens. The hardening moved the checks into the service layer, so now they are refused on every path.
